passages.title: The Tourist Paradox
passages.text: Tourism is often celebrated as one of the most effective ways of bringing prosperity to places that have few other sources of income. Visitors spend money in hotels, restaurants and markets, and the resulting jobs can keep young people from leaving in search of work elsewhere. Yet in a growing number of destinations, residents have begun to speak of a darker side. In some historic city centres, the number of short-term holiday rentals has risen so sharply that long-term residents can no longer afford to live there. Traditional shops have been replaced by souvenir stalls, and the very character that attracted visitors in the first place risks disappearing. This is the paradox at the heart of mass tourism: the more successful a destination becomes, the more it may undermine the qualities on which its success depends. Some cities have responded by limiting the number of cruise ships, introducing tourist taxes or restricting new rental licences. Critics argue that such measures risk turning travel into a privilege reserved for the wealthy. Supporters counter that, without them, popular places will be loved to death. Perhaps the most promising approach lies not in keeping tourists out, but in spreading them more evenly, both across the year and across regions that receive few visitors. Countries that are only now opening up to international tourism, including Iraq, are in a position to learn from these experiences. Their challenge will be to welcome visitors in ways that strengthen, rather than erode, the communities and heritage that make them worth visiting.

passages.title: In Praise of Slow Reading
passages.text: We probably read more words each day than any previous generation. Messages, headlines, captions and notifications follow one another in an endless stream, and most of them are read in seconds. Some researchers worry that this constant skimming is gradually changing the way we read everything else. When people are used to scanning screens for key words, they may find it harder to follow a long, complex argument or to lose themselves in a novel. The concern is not that skimming is bad in itself. It is an efficient way to deal with large amounts of information, and skilled readers have always used it. The problem arises when it becomes our only mode of reading. Deep reading, by contrast, involves slowing down, making connections, questioning the author and allowing ourselves to be moved. It is through this kind of attention, many scholars argue, that we develop empathy and the capacity for critical thought. Encouragingly, the ability to read deeply does not appear to vanish; rather, it weakens when it is not used, much like a muscle. Some teachers now set aside time for uninterrupted reading of printed books, while others ask students to annotate texts by hand. Individual readers can do the same, deliberately choosing a demanding book and reading it without a phone within reach. None of this requires rejecting technology. It simply requires recognising that different kinds of reading serve different purposes, and that the slowest kind may be the one we can least afford to lose.
